subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.activity_description: Students examine a working torchlight, toggle the switch, observe whether the lamp glows, then open the torch to identify the components inside — cells, lamp, and switch — and record their observations.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates how to safely open the torch and guides students to name what they see.
Examine the torch, toggle the switch, open it, and list every component they can identify.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows a working torch and asks students what makes the lamp glow, surfacing initial ideas.
Student groups toggle the switch, observe the lamp, then carefully open the torch and examine the interior components.
Groups record a labelled list of every part they find and share one observation with the class.
Teacher consolidates by naming the components — electric cell, lamp, switch, wires — and connects them to the chapter ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the opening unit of the chapter, and the torch provides a concrete, familiar entry point before any formal definitions are introduced. Watch for students who assume the lamp glows because of the battery alone, ignoring the role of the complete path — this is a central misconception the chapter will address. Encourage groups to count the cells and notice that they are arranged end-to-end, as this will become important in the next unit.

periods.activity_description: Students closely examine a single electric cell, identify its positive terminal (metal cap) and negative terminal (metal disc), note their physical features, and sketch the cell with terminal labels.

roles.role_description: Introduces the terms positive and negative terminal and demonstrates where each is located on the cell.
Examine their own cell, locate both terminals, note physical differences, and produce a labelled sketch.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the torch components from the previous unit and focuses attention on the electric cell.
Each student examines a cell, notes the physical features of both terminals, and sketches the cell with labels.
Students share their sketches in pairs and check whether they have identified the same features; discrepancies are discussed.
Teacher confirms correct identification and introduces the plus and minus notation used on cells.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's open-torch observation, this unit narrows focus to a single component. A common error is confusing the larger flat base of the cell with the positive terminal — clarify that the protruding metal cap is positive. Ask students to feel (gently) the difference in shape between the two ends to reinforce the distinction.
materials: One electric cell per student (AA or D-cell)
Notebook or plain paper for sketching

periods.activity_description: Students remove two cells from a torch, reinsert them in different orders and orientations, and observe which arrangements make the lamp glow, discovering that positive-to-negative series arrangement is required.

roles.role_description: Poses the challenge question and circulates to prompt students to record every arrangement they try.
Systematically try different cell orientations, record which arrangements glow or do not glow, and state the rule they derive.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the two-terminal cell and poses the question: does it matter which way the cells face in the torch?
Groups remove cells, insert them in at least four different orientations, and record lamp glow or no-glow for each.
Groups compare results and discuss what pattern determines whether the lamp glows.
Teacher formalises the term 'battery' — two or more cells in series with positive-to-negative connection — and notes the common use of 'battery' for a single cell.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is a natural extension of the previous two units — students now apply their cell knowledge to a multi-cell arrangement. Watch for the misconception that more cells always means a brighter lamp regardless of orientation; only the correct series connection produces the circuit. Prompt groups to articulate the rule in their own words before the teacher provides the formal definition.

periods.activity_title: Inside the Lamp — Filament and Terminals
periods.activity_description: Students examine an incandescent lamp and an LED side by side, identify their terminals and internal features (filament, wire lengths), and record distinguishing observations in a comparison table.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates how to read the terminal markings on an LED (longer wire = positive) and points out the filament in the incandescent lamp.
Examine both lamp types, complete a comparison table of features, and note which lamp has a filament.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the lamp identified inside the torch and introduces both lamp types for comparison.
Groups examine each lamp, identify terminals, look for the filament in the incandescent lamp, and note wire-length difference in the LED.
Groups fill in a two-column comparison table listing physical features of each lamp type.
Class shares observations; teacher establishes that the incandescent lamp's filament glows when hot, while the LED emits light without a filament.

periods.teacher_notes: Students move from examining the cell to examining the lamp, maintaining the component-by-component progression. The most common confusion is treating the two lamp types as interchangeable — highlight that the LED has a directionality (polarity) that the incandescent lamp does not, which will matter when they build circuits in the next unit. Hold the LED up so students can see the wire-length difference clearly.
materials: One incandescent lamp per group (with visible filament)

periods.activity_title: Making the Lamp Glow — First Circuit
periods.activity_description: Students assemble a circuit using a cell, cell holder, incandescent lamp, lamp holder, and wires, testing different arrangements to discover which connections make the lamp glow and which do not.

roles.role_description: Introduces the materials and asks students to design their own connection sequence before touching the wires.
Plan, assemble, and modify connections, recording glowing and non-glowing arrangements and identifying what all glowing arrangements share.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the previous unit's lamp-and-cell knowledge to the challenge: use these materials to make the lamp glow.
Groups try multiple connection arrangements, sketch each one, and mark whether the lamp glowed.
Groups identify the shared feature of all glowing arrangements and articulate it as a rule.
Teacher introduces the term 'complete circuit' and confirms that a continuous path from one terminal of the cell through the lamp and back to the other terminal is required.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the transition from identifying individual components to assembling them into a working system. Students frequently attempt to connect only one terminal of the lamp to the cell — probe this by asking what happens if the path is broken anywhere. Groups that succeed quickly can be asked to deliberately break the path at one point and explain what they observe.

periods.activity_description: Students replace the incandescent lamp in their circuit with an LED and test both connection orientations, discovering that the LED glows only when its longer (positive) wire connects toward the positive terminal of the cell.

roles.role_description: Poses the question of whether an LED cares about direction and asks groups to predict before testing.
Connect the LED in both orientations, record results, and explain why the LED has a polarity requirement.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the working circuit from the previous unit and introduces the LED as a replacement, asking for predictions about direction.
Groups connect the LED in one orientation, observe, then reverse and observe again, recording both results.
Groups write an explanation linking the LED wire-length observation (from unit 4) to the direction result.
Teacher confirms that current flows in one direction in the LED, connecting back to the cell terminal identification from earlier units.

periods.teacher_notes: Students carry forward their working circuit from the previous unit, so the only variable being changed is the lamp type. The most common misconception is that polarity only matters for batteries, not for individual components — the LED directly challenges this. A useful probing question: 'If you were given an unknown LED with no label, how would you determine which wire is positive?'
materials: Working cell-and-wire circuit from previous unit

periods.activity_description: Students construct a simple switch from drawing pins and a safety pin, insert it into their circuit, and test that it controls the lamp — closing the switch completes the circuit and opening it breaks the circuit.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the physical construction of the drawing-pin switch and frames the question of what a switch actually does to the circuit path.
Build the switch, insert it in series in their circuit, toggle it, and record what happens to the lamp in each switch position.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to recall the torch switch from unit 1 and connects that observation to today's investigation of how a switch works internally.
Groups construct the drawing-pin switch and insert it into their working circuit.
Groups toggle the switch, record lamp behaviour in each position, and describe what is physically happening to the circuit path.
Teacher formalises open circuit (switch OFF, gap present, no current) and closed circuit (switch ON, complete path, current flows).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit closes the loop on the torch observation from unit 1, as students now understand the internal mechanism of the switch they toggled at the start. A misconception to watch for is that the switch 'produces' current when closed — clarify that it only completes or breaks the path for current that originates from the cell. In the next unit, students will draw this circuit symbolically, so asking them to sketch the physical layout now will ease that transition.
materials: Small piece of cardboard or wooden block

periods.activity_title: Direction of Current and the Fused Lamp
periods.activity_description: Students learn that conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell through the external circuit, examine a fused lamp to understand how a broken filament stops current flow, and connect these ideas to their assembled circuits.

roles.role_description: Explains the convention for current direction and demonstrates with a fused lamp what a broken filament looks like.
Annotate a sketch of their assembled circuit with arrows showing current direction and note where a break would stop the lamp glowing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the convention that current direction is taken from positive to negative terminal and asks students what they think happens when the filament breaks.
Teacher shows a fused lamp and discusses how the broken filament creates a gap, then students annotate their circuit sketches with current-direction arrows.
Students mark every point in their sketch where a break would stop the lamp, discussing with a partner why each break works.
Class discussion consolidates the idea that an unbroken path is necessary for current to flow and that a fused lamp is one type of break.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds on the constructed circuits of the previous units by adding the conceptual layer of current direction and circuit continuity. Students often confuse the direction of current with the direction electrons actually move — at this stage, the conventional direction (positive to negative) is sufficient; avoid introducing electron flow. Watch for students who annotate arrows in both directions around the loop, as this suggests they have not yet grasped the single-loop nature of a series circuit.
materials: Students' circuit sketches from previous units

periods.activity_description: Students learn the standard symbols for electric cell, battery, incandescent lamp, LED, switch (ON and OFF), and wire, noting the physical logic behind each symbol (e.g., long line = positive terminal, triangle in LED = current direction).

roles.role_description: Presents each symbol alongside the real component it represents and explains the visual logic encoded in the symbol.
Copy each symbol, annotate it with the feature it encodes (e.g., which line is positive), and match symbols to the components they have already handled.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the circuit-building units by asking how we could communicate a circuit design to someone in another school without sending the actual components.
Teacher introduces each symbol one at a time; students copy the symbol, write the component name, and note one physical feature the symbol encodes.
Students attempt to match a set of symbols to component names without looking at their notes, then self-check.
Teacher notes that international bodies (IEC, ANSI, IEEE) standardise these symbols so they are understood universally.

periods.teacher_notes: Students move from physical circuits to symbolic representation in this unit, so anchoring each symbol to the real component they have handled is essential. A common error is drawing the cell symbol with both lines the same length — stress that the longer line is always the positive terminal. In the next unit, students will use these symbols to draw complete circuit diagrams, so fluency with individual symbols now saves time later.

periods.activity_title: Drawing Circuit Diagrams — Incandescent and LED
periods.activity_description: Students draw two complete circuit diagrams using standard symbols: one for a cell, switch, and incandescent lamp circuit, and one for a cell, switch, and LED circuit — correctly indicating LED polarity in the diagram.

roles.role_description: Models how to start a circuit diagram from one terminal and follow the path around the loop, then circulates to check for errors.
Draw both circuit diagrams independently, annotate current direction with arrows, and mark the positive terminal of the cell.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the process of drawing a circuit diagram by tracing the physical circuit path and replacing each component with its symbol.
Students draw the incandescent lamp circuit diagram, including switch in both open and closed positions as two separate diagrams.
Students draw the LED circuit diagram, paying attention to the triangle direction in the LED symbol to indicate current polarity.
Pairs swap diagrams and check each other's work against the symbol reference; teacher addresses the most common errors whole-class.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the productive application of the previous unit's symbol learning, so students should have their symbol notes available. The most frequent error is drawing the LED symbol without correctly orienting the triangle relative to the current-direction arrow — remind students that the triangle's base faces the incoming current. Prompt students who finish early to draw the switch in both positions to reinforce the open/closed distinction.

periods.activity_title: Reading a Circuit Diagram — Predict, Then Build
periods.activity_description: Students are given an unfamiliar circuit diagram and asked to predict whether the lamp would glow, identify each component, state the switch position, then build the circuit to verify their prediction.

roles.role_description: Provides a circuit diagram that includes a deliberate feature (e.g., LED connected in reverse polarity) and asks students to predict behaviour before building.
Read the diagram, predict lamp behaviour and explain their reasoning, then assemble the circuit and compare the outcome to their prediction.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the unfamiliar circuit diagram and asks groups to write a prediction with a reason before touching any materials.
Groups analyse the diagram — identifying components, noting switch position, checking LED orientation — and record their prediction.
Groups build the circuit from the diagram and observe the actual outcome, then compare to their prediction.
Class discusses cases where prediction and outcome differed, with teacher connecting errors back to symbol-reading rules from the previous two units.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to reverse their process — reading a diagram to predict a physical outcome, rather than drawing a diagram from a physical circuit. This is a more demanding use of circuit diagrams and will surface students who have memorised symbols without understanding what they represent. If most groups predicted incorrectly, revisit the LED polarity symbol before moving on; the next stage requires confident symbol reading.
materials: Printed or teacher-drawn circuit diagram (one per group)
Electric cell, lamp holder, lamp, LED, switch, wires for circuit assembly

periods.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
periods.activity_description: Students construct a conduction tester — a circuit with a cell, lamp, and two free wire ends — and use it to test a range of classroom objects, recording whether each completes the circuit and causes the lamp to glow.

roles.role_description: Introduces the conduction tester concept and asks students to predict which objects will glow the lamp before testing.
Assemble the tester, record predictions, test each object, and fill in a results table with glow / no-glow outcomes.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the switch investigation — where a gap stops current — to the question of whether the gap can be bridged by different materials, motivating the tester design.
Groups assemble the conduction tester and test their first five objects, recording results.
Groups test remaining objects and complete their results table with at least eight entries.
Groups write a preliminary grouping of their objects into two categories based on lamp behaviour, without yet using the formal terms.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit launches the final stage of the chapter by connecting the complete-circuit concept from earlier units to a new investigation context. Students may assume that all shiny objects are conductors — test a piece of glass or a wax candle to challenge this. Encourage groups to include unusual objects (a graphite pencil tip, a coin, a rubber band) to generate a richer data set for the classification activity in the next unit.
materials: Assorted test objects: metal spoon, plastic pen, rubber band, glass piece, coin, wooden stick, paper strip, graphite pencil tip, wax

periods.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
periods.activity_title: Sorting the Evidence — Conductors and Insulators
periods.activity_description: Students sort their conduction-tester results into two groups, apply the formal terms 'conductor' and 'insulator', identify the material pattern across each group, and generate a rule about which material types allow current to flow.

roles.role_description: Introduces the formal vocabulary of conductor and insulator after students have already sorted their data, anchoring the terms to observed evidence.
Re-examine their results table, sort all objects, look for material patterns within each group, and state a rule that predicts which new materials would be conductors.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks groups to share their preliminary two-category groupings from the previous unit before any formal terms are introduced.
Groups sort all tested objects into the two formal categories and identify the material pattern (metals mostly conduct; plastic, rubber, glass, wood mostly do not).
Groups write a predictive rule: 'If a material is ___, we predict it will conduct because ___' and apply it to two untested materials.
Class shares rules; teacher addresses borderline cases and notes that the human body is a conductor, introducing the safety implication.

periods.teacher_notes: Students arrive with data from the previous unit, so this unit is about making meaning from that data rather than gathering more. Watch for overgeneralisation — students sometimes conclude 'all metals conduct' without acknowledging that the test only covered the metals they tried. The human body as conductor is a factual point from the chapter that has genuine safety relevance; treat it seriously but without causing anxiety.
materials: Completed results table from previous unit
Notebook for writing the predictive rule

periods.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
periods.activity_title: Why Wires Have Coverings — Roles of Conductors and Insulators
periods.activity_description: Students examine the design of an electrical wire (conducting core with insulating covering) and explain why conductors are used for specific circuit components and insulators are used as coverings, linking each material choice to its functional role.

roles.role_description: Shows a cut cross-section of an electrical wire and asks students to identify conductor and insulator in the structure before explaining the reason for each.
Annotate a diagram of a wire cross-section with material type and functional role, then answer: what would happen if the covering were also a conductor?

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows a wire cross-section and asks students to apply their conductor/insulator classification from the previous unit to identify each part.
Teacher explains the functional logic: the metal core conducts current along the intended path; the plastic or rubber covering prevents current from taking unintended paths.
Students annotate the wire diagram and answer the counterfactual question about a conducting covering, writing their response in full sentences.
Class discussion surfaces the electric-shock safety point and connects back to the chapter's safety caution about the human body being a conductor.

periods.teacher_notes: Students have classified materials empirically; this unit asks them to use that classification to reason about design choices in real electrical components. The counterfactual question — what if the covering conducted — is the key cognitive move here, pushing from classification into causal reasoning. Ensure students connect their answer to the human-body-as-conductor point from the previous unit, since that is where the safety argument becomes concrete.
materials: Cut cross-section of an electrical wire (or diagram)

periods.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
periods.activity_title: DC and AC — Where Does the Current Come From?
periods.activity_description: Students examine two circuit scenarios — one powered by a cell (DC) and one described as coming from a power plant (AC) — and classify the source type, explain the difference in current direction, and connect this to the conductors and insulators used in each context.

roles.role_description: Introduces the DC/AC distinction from the chapter's Dive Deeper box and poses scenario questions for student analysis.
Classify each scenario as DC or AC, write the key difference in current behaviour, and discuss why insulation is critical for the higher-voltage AC context.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the Bhakra Nangal Dam context from the chapter's opening and asks where household electricity comes from, connecting the power plant to the AC concept.
Teacher presents the DC/AC distinction and students classify three or four given scenarios as DC or AC with a brief justification.
Groups discuss why insulation requirements might differ for AC from a power plant compared to DC from a cell, and write their reasoning.
Teacher consolidates: DC flows in one direction; AC alternates. Both require conductors to carry current and insulators to contain it safely.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit connects the chapter's Dive Deeper content to the conductor/insulator work students have been doing, and also completes the narrative arc from the dam visit that opened the chapter. Students sometimes think AC and DC are different substances rather than different patterns of current behaviour — clarify that it is the same kind of current, just flowing differently. This unit also sets up the final unit's integrative task.
materials: Scenario cards or written scenarios (DC cell torch, AC household socket, AC power plant, DC battery-powered device)

periods.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
periods.activity_title: Design a Safe Circuit — Putting It All Together
periods.activity_description: Students are given a fault-finding scenario: a described circuit uses the wrong materials in certain positions (e.g., a rubber strip as a connecting wire, bare uninsulated wires exposed to touch) and they must identify each fault, classify the material as conductor or insulator, and justify a correction.

roles.role_description: Presents the faulty circuit scenario and asks students to approach it as a fault-finding investigation rather than a recall task.
Identify each fault in the described circuit, state whether conductor or insulator is in the wrong position, and propose a corrected circuit description with justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the faulty circuit scenario and asks groups to first draw the circuit as described before evaluating it.
Groups analyse the circuit, identify each fault, classify the misplaced material, and link the fault to a consequence (lamp will not glow / shock risk).
Groups write a corrected circuit description, specifying the correct material type for each component position and the reason for the correction.
Groups present their corrections; teacher draws out the full arc from component identification through circuit construction to material classification as the backbone of the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the closing unit of the chapter, and the fault-finding format requires students to draw on all four stages of learning: identifying components, understanding complete circuits, reading and drawing circuit diagrams, and classifying materials. Watch for groups that correct the conductor/insulator faults but miss the circuit-continuity faults, as this suggests they have compartmentalised knowledge rather than integrated it. The brief closing arc review is a natural moment to surface connections students may not have made explicitly during earlier units.
materials: Faulty circuit scenario description (written on board or distributed as handout)

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine a torchlight and its internal components, identify the terminals of an electric cell, discover the series arrangement required in a battery, and compare the physical features of incandescent lamps and LEDs.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe the physical features and terminals of an electric cell, battery, incandescent lamp, and LED, and state the correct series arrangement of cells in a battery.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students assemble circuits using cells, lamps, and switches, test LED polarity, construct a simple switch, and trace conventional current direction — learning that a continuous, unbroken path is required for current to flow.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a working simple circuit using a cell, lamp, and switch, explain why the circuit must be complete for the lamp to glow, and demonstrate that an LED allows current in one direction only.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students learn standard symbols for all circuit components, draw circuit diagrams for incandescent and LED circuits, and read an unfamiliar circuit diagram to predict and verify circuit behaviour.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can draw and read circuit diagrams using standard symbols for cells, batteries, lamps, LEDs, switches, and wires, and use a circuit diagram to predict whether a lamp will glow.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify materials as conductors or insulators and explain their roles
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build and use a conduction tester to classify materials as conductors or insulators, explain the functional roles of each in circuit design and wire construction, distinguish DC from AC, and apply their knowledge to identify and correct faults in a described circuit.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as conductors or insulators using evidence from a conduction test, explain why conductors and insulators are each used in specific positions within electrical components, and describe how electricity flows through simple circuits by manipulating circuit components.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and describe the physical features and terminals of an electric cell, battery, incandescent lamp, and LED, and state the correct series arrangement of cells in a battery.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: Which terminal of an electric cell is represented by the metal cap that protrudes from one end?

options.label: A
options.text: The negative terminal, marked –

options.label: B
options.text: The neutral terminal, which connects to the filament

options.label: C
options.text: The output terminal, from which current leaves only when a switch is closed

options.label: D
options.text: The positive terminal, marked +

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has reversed the terminal identification, confusing the flat metal disc (negative) with the protruding cap.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has imported an unrelated concept (neutral terminal) not present in the chapter, possibly from household electricity knowledge.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates the terminal's identity with switch-dependent behaviour, showing a misconception that the terminal's nature changes with circuit state.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with text labels may be shown the physical cell and asked to point to the terminal; students who answer correctly can be asked to explain the marking convention.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and describe the physical features and terminals of an electric cell, battery, incandescent lamp, and LED, and state the correct series arrangement of cells in a battery.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: A student inserts two cells into a torch so that the positive terminal of the first cell faces the positive terminal of the second cell. What will happen when the switch is pressed?

options.label: A
options.text: The lamp will glow briefly and then stop because the cells cancel each other's energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The lamp will glow more brightly because both positive terminals face the same direction.

options.label: C
options.text: The lamp will glow normally because the switch completes the circuit regardless of cell orientation.

options.label: D
options.text: The lamp will not glow because the cells are not in the correct series arrangement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student believes same-polarity alignment boosts output, not recognising that the positive-to-negative series arrangement is required for the circuit to function.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student thinks the switch is the sole determinant of lamp behaviour, not understanding the role of cell orientation in completing the circuit.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has a partial grasp that something is wrong but applies an incorrect energy-cancellation model not grounded in the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to draw the two cells end-to-end and label the terminals they can see; this externalises the reasoning and often resolves the confusion.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a working simple circuit using a cell, lamp, and switch, explain why the circuit must be complete for the lamp to glow, and demonstrate that an LED allows current in one direction only.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: A student builds a circuit with a cell, an incandescent lamp, and a switch. The lamp glows when the switch is closed. The student then opens the switch. Which statement correctly explains why the lamp stops glowing?

options.label: A
options.text: Opening the switch causes the filament to cool instantly, preventing it from reaching the required temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Opening the switch creates a gap in the circuit, breaking the path for current.

options.label: C
options.text: Opening the switch disconnects the cell, removing its stored energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Opening the switch reverses the current direction, which cancels the lamp's glow.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates the switch with the cell, not understanding that the switch controls the path, not the energy source.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has imported a current-reversal idea not present in the chapter, possibly confusing AC behaviour with switch action.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student focuses on a consequence (cooling filament) rather than the cause (broken path); this is a partial understanding that misses the circuit-continuity principle.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the explanation may draw the circuit and physically trace where the gap appears when the switch opens; this spatial approach often clarifies the concept.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a working simple circuit using a cell, lamp, and switch, explain why the circuit must be complete for the lamp to glow, and demonstrate that an LED allows current in one direction only.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: A student connects an LED in a circuit with a cell. The LED does not glow. The student then reverses the LED's connections and the LED glows. What does this show about the LED?

options.label: A
options.text: The LED allows current to flow in one direction only, so its polarity must match the cell's terminals.

options.label: B
options.text: The LED glows only when the incandescent lamp is also present in the circuit.

options.label: C
options.text: The LED requires a battery of two cells to glow; a single cell is insufficient.

options.label: D
options.text: The LED's longer wire is always connected to the negative terminal for it to glow.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student attributes the failure to the cell count rather than polarity, conflating the battery-capacity concept from section 3.2.2 with LED directionality.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has reversed the polarity rule: the chapter states the longer wire is the positive terminal, to be connected toward the positive terminal of the cell.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student introduces a dependency between lamp types not described in the chapter, reflecting a confusion between the two lamp types explored in the activities.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to sketch the two LED orientations and mark which wire (longer or shorter) faces the cell's positive terminal in each, making the polarity rule visible.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a working simple circuit using a cell, lamp, and switch, explain why the circuit must be complete for the lamp to glow, and demonstrate that an LED allows current in one direction only.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: A student builds a circuit with a cell, an incandescent lamp, and a homemade switch using a safety pin and drawing pins. Describe TWO changes the student could make to the switch that would prevent the lamp from glowing even when the switch appears to be in the closed position.
expected_elements: Removing one of the drawing pins so the safety pin cannot bridge the gap, creating an open circuit even when the pin is touching one pin only.
Using a non-conducting material (such as rubber or plastic) in place of the metal drawing pins, so the bridge does not allow current to pass even when contact is made.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to generate two changes may first describe what makes the switch work, then reason backwards about what would stop it; offering this prompting sequence allows students with strong conceptual understanding but weaker verbal expression to show their thinking.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can draw and read circuit diagrams using standard symbols for cells, batteries, lamps, LEDs, switches, and wires, and use a circuit diagram to predict whether a lamp will glow.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.question_text: In the standard symbol for an electric cell used in circuit diagrams, two lines represent the two terminals. Which statement correctly describes these lines?

options.label: A
options.text: Both lines are the same length; the terminal identity is shown by the + and – labels only.

options.label: B
options.text: The longer line represents the positive terminal and the shorter line represents the negative terminal.

options.label: C
options.text: The longer line represents the terminal from which conventional current exits the external circuit.

options.label: D
options.text: The shorter line represents the positive terminal and the longer line represents the negative terminal.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has reversed the line-length convention, a common error when symbols are drawn from memory without checking the encoding rule.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student believes the symbol requires written labels rather than encoding polarity in line length, missing the purpose of standardised symbols.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has the correct line (longer = positive) but states the function incorrectly; conventional current exits the positive terminal into the external circuit, so this is partially right but worded in a way that could confuse current direction.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be directed to compare the cell symbol to the physical cell they handled — the longer line corresponds to the longer, protruding positive terminal — using this physical anchor to ground the symbolic convention.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can draw and read circuit diagrams using standard symbols for cells, batteries, lamps, LEDs, switches, and wires, and use a circuit diagram to predict whether a lamp will glow.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works through manipulating different elements in simple circuits and demonstrate the heating and magnetic effects of electricity.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Component | Symbol feature | What the feature encodes
Electric cell | Long line and short line | Long line = positive terminal
LED | Triangle pointing in one direction with two arrows | Triangle direction = direction of current flow; arrows = light emission
Switch (open) | Gap in the connecting line | Gap = circuit is broken, no current flows
Switch (closed) | Continuous line with bridging element | Continuous path = circuit is complete
assessment_items.question_text: A student reads a circuit diagram for a cell, LED, and switch. The LED symbol's triangle points away from the positive terminal of the cell. Refer to the table provided. Predict whether the LED will glow when the switch is closed, and give one reason from the table.

options.label: A
options.text: The LED will glow because the switch is closed and a complete path exists regardless of the LED's orientation.

options.label: B
options.text: The LED will glow because the two arrows in the LED symbol indicate it emits light in any direction of current.

options.label: C
options.text: The LED will not glow because an open-switch symbol is present in the diagram.

options.label: D
options.text: The LED will not glow because the triangle direction shows current must flow toward the LED's positive connection, but the diagram places the LED in reverse polarity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student treats circuit completeness (closed switch) as sufficient for the LED to glow, having not integrated the polarity requirement from the LED symbol's triangle direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student misreads the diagram — no open switch was stated — suggesting difficulty reading and integrating multiple symbol features simultaneously.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student misinterprets the two arrows as indicating bidirectional light emission that overrides polarity, confusing the light-emission symbol with a direction-independence claim.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to reason from the table can first draw the circuit from the description, then use arrows to trace the current path and check whether it aligns with the triangle in the LED symbol.

assessment_items.question_text: Draw a circuit diagram for a circuit that contains: one electric cell, one switch in the open position, and one incandescent lamp. Label the positive terminal of the cell. Add an arrow to show the direction conventional current would flow if the switch were closed.
expected_elements: Correct symbol used for the electric cell, with the longer line identified or labelled as positive.
Correct symbol used for the switch, drawn in the open position (gap visible in the symbol).
Correct symbol used for the incandescent lamp.
All three components connected in a single closed loop by lines representing wires.
A current-direction arrow added somewhere on the loop, pointing from the positive terminal of the cell through the external circuit toward the negative terminal.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find drawing symbols precisely difficult may describe the diagram in words (e.g., 'long line, short line for cell; line with gap for switch; circle with X for lamp; arrow pointing from long-line side') — verbal description of the correct structure demonstrates the same understanding as a drawn diagram.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Object tested | Lamp glows?
Copper coin | Yes
Rubber band | No
Graphite pencil tip | Yes
Wooden stick | No
Aluminium foil | Yes
Glass piece | No

assessment_items.question_text: A student uses a conduction tester to test eight objects. Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

options.label: A
options.text: All metals and graphite in the table conducted electricity, while all non-metals except graphite did not.

options.label: B
options.text: All objects that are solids conducted electricity, while those that are soft or flexible did not.

options.label: C
options.text: All shiny objects conducted electricity, while all dull objects did not.

options.label: D
options.text: Hard objects conducted electricity, while soft objects did not.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is using a visual property (shininess) rather than material type, a common overgeneralisation when metals are the most familiar conductors.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is using a physical property (hardness) not supported by the data — graphite conducts but is soft and brittle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is applying a solid-vs-flexible rule that the data does not support — wax and wood are solids that do not conduct.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to separate the table rows that glow from those that do not, then look for the material-type pattern by naming what each glowing object is made of.

assessment_items.question_text: An electrical wire has a copper core surrounded by a plastic covering. A student suggests replacing the plastic covering with a thin copper covering to make the wire look metallic. What would happen to the circuit if this change were made, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Anyone who touches the outer surface of the wire could receive an electric shock, because the copper covering would conduct current to the person's body.

options.label: B
options.text: The circuit would stop working because copper coverings prevent current from reaching the inner core.

options.label: C
options.text: The circuit would work normally because both the inner core and the outer covering are made of the same material.

options.label: D
options.text: The lamp in the circuit would glow more brightly because two copper conductors carry more current than one.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has reversed the role of the covering — thinking it blocks current from the core — showing a misunderstanding of what insulation does vs. what the conducting core does.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student believes more conductor material means more current, confusing conductor area with current magnitude in a way the chapter does not support.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student knows the circuit would function (current still flows through the core) but misses the safety consequence of an exposed conducting surface, separating electrical function from safety reasoning.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be directed to recall from their conductor classification that the human body is listed as a conductor — this link often unlocks the safety reasoning needed to evaluate the outer copper covering.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to build a torchlight using only materials available at home. She has: two AA cells, a small incandescent lamp with a holder, two lengths of copper wire stripped of their plastic covering, one length of copper wire still covered in plastic, a metal safety pin, and two drawing pins. Describe how she should assemble the circuit, explaining at each step why the chosen material is correct for that position. Include in your answer: the arrangement of the cells, how the switch should be constructed, and what role the plastic covering plays.
look_for: Correctly states that the two cells must be arranged in series — positive terminal of one cell touching the negative terminal of the other — and explains this is required for the battery to provide energy to the circuit.
Specifies that the stripped copper wires (conductors) are used to connect components, because they allow current to flow through the intended path.
Describes the switch as the safety pin bridging two drawing pins inserted in a non-conducting surface, and explains that when the pin touches both drawing pins, it closes the circuit.

Explains that the plastic-covered wire should be avoided for internal connections but could be used where the wire must be touched — because the plastic insulator prevents current from reaching the person's hand.
Traces the complete current path from the positive terminal of the battery, through the lamp, through the switch, and back to the negative terminal, using the conventional current direction.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with extended writing can be invited to draw the circuit and annotate each component with its material, role (conductor or insulator), and reason for placement — the annotated drawing is an equally valid demonstration of the same reasoning.

assessment_items.task: A student has built a circuit with four faults. Refer to the table provided. For each fault: (1) state whether the faulty part is a conductor or an insulator, (2) state what type of material should replace it, and (3) explain in one sentence why that correction is necessary for the circuit to work safely.
assessment_items.scaffold: Work through each row of the table one at a time. For each fault, ask: Should current flow through this part or be blocked? Then decide: should it be a conductor or an insulator? Finally, connect your correction to either circuit function (lamp will/will not glow) or safety (shock risk).
format_of_output: Completed table with all four rows filled in
One justification sentence per row in the 'Why the correction is necessary' column

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Procedure evaluation task (identify flaw, suggest improvement)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires students to both classify materials and explain their functional roles in circuits; a fault-finding table requires both operations simultaneously — classifying the faulty material and reasoning about the consequence — making it the most direct demonstration vehicle.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can apply conductor/insulator classification to evaluate real circuit-design choices, reason about the consequences of incorrect material placement (both functional and safety), and connect cell-orientation knowledge to circuit behaviour — the full range of the chapter's central cognitive operation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to focus on one row at a time and use the functional question (should current flow here or not?) as the reasoning entry point — this prevents students from guessing material types without justification. Faults 1 and 2 test conductor/insulator reasoning for circuit function; Fault 3 tests safety reasoning; Fault 4 tests cell-arrangement knowledge from the first stage.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly classify all four faulty parts, specify the replacement material type precisely (e.g., 'a metal conductor' not just 'a better material'), and write justification sentences that name a consequence (lamp will not glow / shock risk). Weak responses either misclassify the faulty material or write justifications that are tautological ('it should be a conductor because conductors conduct') without naming a circuit-function or safety consequence.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the table format can describe each correction verbally or draw the corrected circuit and annotate the changed parts — what matters is that both the classification and the justification are present; the format of their response is secondary.
